title: In what is the effect of negative number in field
subject: C Programming
text: In C, what is the effect of a negative number in a field width specifier?

options.html: the values are displayed as negative numbers

solution:
Concept: In C's printf-family functions, a field width specifies the minimum number of characters printed for a value, with the remaining space filled by padding. A positive width right-justifies the value by default (padding added on the left). A negative width — which can only arise when the width is supplied via the * width argument — is defined by the C standard to be interpreted as the - (left-justify) flag combined with the absolute value of that width: it forces left-justified output, with padding added on the right instead.

Application: Trace a concrete case:

  1. Consider printf("[%5d]", 7) — the width 5 is positive, so the default (right-justified) alignment applies: it prints [ 7].

  2. Now consider printf("[%*d]", -5, 7) — the width argument passed is -5, a negative number.

  3. Per the format-specifier rule, that negative sign is stripped off to get an actual width of 5, and the - (left-justify) flag is activated because the supplied width was negative.

  4. The output therefore becomes [7 ] — left-justified, with the padding spaces moved to the right of the value.

Cross-check: This matches the ISO C standard (WG14 N1570 §7.21.6.1) and the POSIX printf specification, both of which state that a negative width argument is taken as the - flag with a positive width. It also rules out the other options: printf's format specifiers have no centering capability at all (ruling out center-alignment), and the field width never changes the sign of the printed value — only its alignment and padding (ruling out the "displayed as negative numbers" option).

Result: A negative field width specifier causes the value to be displayed left-justified.

optionFeedback.html: Right-justified output is what printf produces by default when the field width is given as an ordinary positive value — it is not what happens when the width is negative, which is a distinct, explicitly different case in the format specification.

printf's field-width mechanism only ever controls whether padding goes on the left or the right of a value; centering text within a field is not a capability that the standard C library's format specifiers provide at all.

A negative value supplied to printf's field width via the * width argument — e.g. printf("%*d", -5, 7) — is defined by the C standard to be treated as the - (left-justify) flag combined with the absolute value as the actual width. So the output is left-justified, with padding added on the right instead of the left.

The field-width specifier only ever controls the spacing and alignment used around the printed representation of a value; it has no effect whatsoever on the sign of the number itself, so a negative width cannot turn a positive value into a negative-looking one.

title: What is the output when the following segment of code
subject: C Programming
text:
What is the output when the following segment of ‘C’ code is executed?

void main()
{
    float a = 123.456;
    printf("%.2f, %7.3f, %12e", a, a, a);
}
solution:
Concept — how a printf conversion is built

A conversion specification here has the form %[flags][width][.precision]conversion; optional flags may also appear right after the % sign, and none of the three conversions in this call uses one. The width is a minimum total field width: with no flag, if the converted text is shorter, spaces are added on the left, and if it is already that long or longer nothing is added — printf never truncates a number to make it fit. The .precision is the count of digits printed after the decimal point for both f and e; it defaults to 6, and the value is rounded to that many digits, never cut. An e conversion also normalises the number as d.dddddde±dd, that is, one non-zero digit before the point.

Application — the three conversions in this call, with a = 123.456

  1. %.2f: no width is given and the precision is 2, so 123.456 is rounded to two decimal digits — the third digit 6 rounds the 5 up — giving 123.46.

  2. %7.3f: the precision 3 gives 123.456, and that text is already 7 characters long (three digits, the point, three more digits), so the minimum width of 7 is exactly met and no spaces are added.

  3. %12e: no precision is written, so the default 6 applies — mantissa 1.234560 and exponent 2, that is 1.234560 × 102, written 1.234560e+02. Count its characters: one digit, the point, six digits, the letter e, the sign and two exponent digits — 12 in all. The minimum width of 12 is exactly met, so here too no spaces are added.

So the widths 7 and 12 only reserve room; here the text already fills them, which is why no padding appears. Had the call used %15e, the same 12-character text would have been printed with three leading spaces, and %9.3f would print two leading spaces before 123.456. Without a flag, a width can only add spaces on the left — it never adds digits and never cuts; a - flag would left-justify the text instead, and 0 would pad it with zeros.

One more detail: a is declared float, and a float argument is promoted to double before printf reads it. 123.456 is not exactly representable in binary, so the stored value is about 123.456001, but at 2, 3 and 6 decimal digits it still rounds to the digits shown.

Result: the three fields print as 123.46, 123.456, 1.234560e+02.

title: <iostream> using namespace std; int void fun() int int cout
subject: C Programming
text:
What is the output of the following C++ program?

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
int x = 10;
void fun() {
    int x = 2;
    {
        int x = 1;
        cout << ::x << endl;
    }
}
int main() {
    fun();
    return 0;
}
solution:
Concept

The unary scope resolution operator :: (with nothing on its left) always names an identifier from the global namespace. It bypasses every local or block-scope declaration that may be shadowing the same name, so it is unaffected by any inner variable of the same name.

Application

  1. A global variable x is defined at file scope with value 10.

  2. Inside fun() a local x = 2 shadows the global, and an inner block declares yet another x = 1 that shadows both. These two only affect an unqualified x.

  3. The print statement is cout << ::x << endl;. Because the name is qualified with ::, lookup goes straight to the global x, ignoring the block-scoped 1 and the function-scoped 2.

  4. Hence the value sent to cout is the global value, 10.

Cross-check

The code is syntactically valid C++, so it compiles and runs cleanly. If the same line were written as an unqualified cout << x it would instead print the nearest enclosing local, 1; the :: prefix is exactly what forces the global value, 10.

optionFeedback.html: Picking 1 assumes ::x refers to the innermost block-scoped x, whose value is 1. But the :: prefix is a qualified name, not a plain x, so it does not denote that inner block variable at all. This value comes from misreading which x the qualified name selects.

Picking 2 assumes ::x refers to the x = 2 local to fun(). A qualified name written with :: is not the same identifier as the unqualified function-local x, so that local is not what this expression denotes. This choice mistakes which x the qualified name selects.

The qualified name ::x resolves to the global variable defined at file scope, whose value is 10, independent of the shadowing locals inside the function and block. That global value is what cout prints.

The program is well-formed C++: redeclaring x in nested scopes is legal shadowing, not a redefinition error, and the global scope operator is used correctly. There is nothing to make compilation or execution fail.

title: Which of the following is wrong about the data types?
subject: C Programming
text: Which of the following statements about data types is wrong?

options.html: The number is always positive when the qualifier 'unsigned' is used.
The number can be positive or negative when the qualifier 'signed' is used.
The range of values for signed data types is more than that of unsigned data types.
The leftmost bit in an unsigned data type is used to represent the value.

solution:
Concept

A data type's storage is a fixed number of bits, and that width fixes the total count of distinct values it can hold (2^n for n bits). 'signed' versus 'unsigned' does not change how many values exist — it only changes which values those bit-patterns are mapped to. A signed type dedicates one bit to recording the sign, so its patterns are split between negative and non-negative numbers; an unsigned type uses every bit for magnitude, so all its patterns are non-negative.

Applying it to each statement

Read every statement and decide whether it is true; the question asks for the one that is wrong.

  • Unsigned removes the sign, so it cannot store a negative number (it stores non-negative values) — a true description of unsigned behaviour.

  • Signed reserves a sign bit, so it can store both negative and non-negative numbers — a true description of signed behaviour.

  • Signed has a greater range than unsigned — this is the claim to test below.

  • In unsigned, no bit is reserved for a sign, so every bit (including the leftmost) carries magnitude — a true description.

Cross-check the range claim with an 8-bit example

  1. Unsigned 8-bit uses all 8 bits for magnitude: it covers 0 to 255, so its maximum value is 255.

  2. Signed 8-bit (two's complement) spends one bit on the sign: it covers -128 to 127, so its maximum value is 127.

  3. Both hold 2^8 = 256 distinct values, but the unsigned maximum (255) is larger than the signed maximum (127).

Result

Because the unsigned type reaches a higher maximum value for the same width, the statement claiming that signed types have a larger range than unsigned types does not hold. The other three statements correctly describe how signed and unsigned types behave.

optionFeedback.html: This statement concerns the unsigned qualifier. Removing the sign means none of the bit-patterns map to a negative number, so the values it can hold run over zero and the positive numbers — that is, the non-negative range starting at zero.

This statement concerns the signed qualifier. One bit is set aside to record the sign, so the remaining bit-patterns are split between negative numbers on one side and zero with the positive numbers on the other — covering both negative and non-negative values.

This statement concerns the comparative range of signed and unsigned types. For a fixed bit width a signed type uses one bit for the sign, lowering its maximum magnitude, while an unsigned type uses every bit for magnitude; so for the same width it is the unsigned type that attains the larger maximum value, and the direction of the comparison given here runs opposite to that.

This statement concerns bit usage in an unsigned type. With no bit reserved for a sign, every bit — the most-significant (leftmost) bit included — contributes to the magnitude that the pattern represents.

title: Consider the following code. #include #include void main() double pi

text:
Consider the following C code:

#include <math.h>
void main()
{
 double pi = 3.1415926535;
 int a = 1;
 int i;
 for(i=0; i < 3; i++)
 if(a = cos(pi * i/2) )
 printf("%d ",1);
 else printf("%d ", 0);
}

solution:
Concept

  • An unbraced loop or if/else governs exactly ONE statement. A complete if/else is itself a single statement, so a for loop with no braces legally controls the entire if/else as its single body.

  • In a condition, '=' is ASSIGNMENT, not comparison. if(a = expr) stores expr into a and then tests a's value; any non-zero result is true, zero is false.

  • Assigning a double to an int variable TRUNCATES toward zero (drops the fractional part); the int's value, not the original double, is what gets tested.

Applying it

Here a is an int, so cos(...) is truncated to an int before the truthiness test. The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2:

  1. i = 0: cos(0) = 1.0 -> a = 1 -> non-zero (true) -> prints 1

  2. i = 1: cos(pi/2) is a tiny value near zero (pi is slightly less than the true value, so it is about 0.00000000004, not exactly 0) -> truncated to int 0 -> zero (false) -> prints 0

  3. i = 2: cos(pi) = -1.0 -> a = -1 -> non-zero (true) -> prints 1

Cross-check

Note the catch at i = 1: the double result is not literally 0, yet because a is an int the fractional value is truncated to 0, which is what makes the test false. Concatenating the three printed digits with spaces gives the output 1 0 1, i.e. 101.

optionFeedback.html: This result would need the assigned cosine value to be treated as false on every iteration. But assigning a non-zero number to the int makes the condition true, so an all-false outcome misreads how non-zero results behave in a C condition.

This mixes up which iterations are true and false by assuming a non-zero cosine result can act as false. In C any non-zero value in the condition is true, so this reading of the iterations is incorrect.
With the cosine result assigned to an int, a non-zero value gives true and a value that truncates to int 0 gives false; running the three iterations in order produces the digits 1 0 1.

This assumes the cosine result is non-zero on every iteration. One value is a tiny fraction near zero that, once stored in the int, truncates to 0 and becomes false - overlooking double-to-int truncation is the mistake.

What is the value of i at the end of the pseudocode?
solution:
Tracing a while-loop means evaluating the guard condition before every pass and updating every variable using the values already computed so far. A self-referential assignment like x := 2^x always uses the OLD value of x to compute the NEW value of x. The loop terminates the first time the guard evaluates to false, checked at the top of each pass before any further update happens.

  1. Initial values: x = 1, i = 1.

  2. Guard check: x = 1 ≤ 1000 is true, so the loop runs. Update: x := 2^1 = 2; i := 1 + 1 = 2.

  3. Guard check: x = 2 ≤ 1000 is true. Update: x := 2^2 = 4; i := 2 + 1 = 3.

  4. Guard check: x = 4 ≤ 1000 is true. Update: x := 2^4 = 16; i := 3 + 1 = 4.

  5. Guard check: x = 16 ≤ 1000 is true. Update: x := 2^16 = 65,536; i := 4 + 1 = 5.

  6. Guard check: x = 65,536 ≤ 1000 is false, so the loop exits without any further update.

The pseudocode ends with i = 5.

The jump from x = 16 to x = 65,536 vastly overshoots the threshold in a single step, so the same trace still ends at i = 5 even for nearby threshold variants (for example, x ≤ 500 or x ≤ 2000) — the result depends only on the doubly-exponential growth of the sequence 1, 2, 4, 16, 65536, not on the exact limit value.

optionFeedback.html: This matches counting only the first three self-referential updates of x (1 → 2 → 4 → 16) and stopping there without re-checking the loop guard against the newest value of x. The condition x ≤ 1000 must be re-evaluated using the CURRENT x after every update, and 16 still satisfies it, so the loop has not yet terminated at this point.

Tracing the self-referential update x := 2^x from the starting values x = 1, i = 1 gives x = 2, 4, 16, and then 65,536 after four updates, each one computed using the CURRENT x as the exponent and each followed by an increment of i. The guard x ≤ 1000 first fails once x reaches 65,536, so the loop exits with i four more than its starting value of 1.

This matches checking the loop guard AFTER incrementing i on the pass where x first exceeds the limit, rather than testing the guard BEFORE that pass runs — as though the loop is always allowed to complete whatever pass is already underway even once the updated x is no longer within range. In this pseudocode, the guard is evaluated at the top of every pass, before the body runs, so the loop exits immediately once it is false and nothing inside the body executes on that pass.

This matches compounding two separate slips: crediting the loop with an extra pass for the very first assignment lines (x := 1; i := 1;) as though they themselves count as one turn of the loop, AND continuing to increment i once more after the guard has already failed on the final value of x. Neither the initial assignments nor a failed guard check are turns of the loop body — the body runs, and i increments, only for passes where the guard was true at the top.

If the break statement is omitted in all the case blocks of a switch control structure, a behavior known as fall-through occurs.

title: What does it mean when we mention prototype of function

subtopic: Function Basics – Definition, Declaration, and Calling Mechanisms
text: What does it mean when we mention prototype of a function in C language?
solution:
In C, before a function is used the compiler needs to know its interface — the function's name, return type, and the type of every parameter it takes. A statement that specifies this interface without supplying the function's body is a function declaration; when that declaration also lists the parameter types (not just the count), it is specifically called a function prototype, as defined in the ISO C standard (C11, sections 6.2.1 and 6.7.6.3).

So mentioning or writing out a function's prototype in source code — stating its return type, name, and parameter types ahead of its use — is exactly the act of declaring that function to the compiler. That is why the correct answer is "Declaring."

  • Prototyping — not a distinct C-language construct or standard term for this act; C programmers and the ISO standard both describe writing the prototype as declaring the function.

  • Calling — happens later, when control and the argument values are handed to an already declared (or defined) function so its code actually runs; mentioning the prototype alone does not run anything.

  • Defining — requires supplying the function's body (the code inside { }); a prototype has no body, so writing one cannot be defining the function.

This also matches how C allows a function to be declared (via its prototype) any number of times across different files before it is defined exactly once — the prototype's entire job is to state the interface, which is precisely what "declaring" means.

optionFeedback.html: "Prototyping" is not a recognized C-language term for this action — it commonly refers to an informal design or engineering mock-up process, not to any construct defined in the ISO C standard or standard C textbooks.

solution:
Concept

The expression n & (n - 1) is a standard bit trick that clears exactly the lowest set (1) bit of n, leaving every higher bit unchanged. A function that repeatedly applies this operation and adds 1 until n becomes 0 is therefore computing the population count -- the number of 1-bits -- of its argument. Separately, in C the binary '-' operator binds tighter than the bitwise '&' operator, so an unparenthesized n & n-1 always parses as n & (n - 1), never as (n & n) - 1.

Application

Tracing res(6) using this rule:

  1. res(6): n is nonzero, so return 1 + res(6 & 5). In binary 6 = 110 and 5 = 101, so 6 & 5 = 100 = 4.

  2. res(4): n is nonzero, so return 1 + res(4 & 3). In binary 4 = 100 and 3 = 011, so 4 & 3 = 000 = 0.

  3. res(0): n is 0, so the base case returns 0 directly.

  4. Unwinding the recursion: res(4) = 1 + 0 = 1, and res(6) = 1 + res(4) = 1 + 1 = 2.

Cross-check

6 in binary is 110, which has exactly two 1-bits, matching the population count of 2 returned by res(6). So printf("%d", res(6)) prints 2. (Note: main calls res before res is declared/defined; this is written the way older, permissive C compilers -- the norm assumed by this class of exam question -- accept, implicitly treating res as a function returning int, so the program compiles and behaves exactly as analyzed above.)

optionFeedback.html: The recursive step 1 + res(n & (n - 1)) clears one set bit from n on every call until n reaches 0, so the function counts the set bits of its argument. For 6 (binary 110), the trace is 6 -> 4 -> 0: two nonzero calls each add 1, so res(6) evaluates to 2 and printf("%d", res(6)) outputs 2.

This matches the result only if 6 had a single set bit to clear. But 6 in binary is 110, which has more than one 1-bit, so more than one recursive step is needed before n reaches 0 -- making 1 too small a count.

This treats res's return value as equal to its input argument. But res is defined by a base case plus a recursive step, not as an identity function -- so the value it prints need not equal the value passed in.

This is only the base-case return, produced when n is already 0. The initial call is res(6), so the function must pass through the recursive branch at least once before it ever reaches that base case.

title: What happens if user dereferences an uninitialised pointer?
subject: C Programming
subtopic: Pointer Basics – Declaration, Initialization, and Dereferencing
text: What happens if a user dereferences an uninitialised pointer?
solution:
Dereferencing an uninitialized pointer in C/C++ results in undefined behavior. It does not cause compilation errors or guarantee zero values, but rather leads to unpredictable program execution.
NOTE
When a local pointer variable is declared in programming languages like C or C++, it is not automatically set to NULL or given a safe default address. Instead, it contains whatever random data happened to be left over in that memory location (often called a garbage value).

If a program attempts to dereference this uninitialized pointer (i.e., read or write the data at the address it holds), it will try to access a completely arbitrary, random location in memory. This actions triggers what the language standards classify as Undefined Behavior (UB).

What Actually Happens at Runtime?

Because the behavior is undefined, anything could happen depending on your operating system, compiler, and current memory layout:

  1. Segmentation Fault / Crash (Most Common): If the random address falls inside memory owned by the operating system or another process, the OS will immediately terminate your program to protect system security.

  2. Silent Data Corruption: If the random address accidentally points to a valid variable elsewhere inside your own program, you might overwrite critical application data without raising any immediate error.

  3. Apparent Normal Operation: Occasionally, the garbage value might happen to point to a harmless, unused memory block, allowing the program to run fine today but crash unpredictably tomorrow on a different machine.

The compiler generally cannot know what arbitrary value will reside in memory at runtime. While modern compilers might throw a warning (e.g., "variable used uninitialized"), it is perfectly valid syntax and will successfully compile into machine code.

The memory is not cleared out automatically. You will only get a zero if the leftover garbage in that specific memory slot happened to be zero by pure luck.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q134
subject: C Programming
text: In C, which of the following is TRUE about arrays and pointers?
solution:
Concept: In C, an array and a pointer are distinct types with independently-determined storage sizes and different lvalue properties, but the language standard defines certain array operations directly in terms of pointer arithmetic. Three governing rules matter here: (1) sizeof (C11 §6.5.3.4) applied to a fixed-size array name yields the array's own total size — element count × element size — computed from its declared type, never a pointer's size; (2) an array name used in an expression decays into a pointer to its first element (C11 §6.3.2.1; except as the operand of sizeof or unary &), but that decayed value is not a modifiable lvalue, so it cannot be the operand of ++; (3) the standard's subscript-operator rule (C11 §6.5.2.1) defines E1[E2] as identical to *((E1) + (E2)) whenever one operand has pointer-to-object type and the other has integer type.

Application: Trace each rule against a concrete declaration, int arr[5]; int *p = arr;:

  1. sizeof check: sizeof(arr) = 5 × sizeof(int) = 20 bytes on a typical platform, computed from the array's own type; sizeof(p) = the pointer's fixed size (commonly 8 bytes on a 64-bit build), computed from the pointer's own type — these are two independent computations, so an array's total size is not guaranteed to match a pointer's size (though for a specific array length and platform the two byte counts could coincidentally match; the standard gives no such guarantee, unlike rule 3 below).

  2. Increment check: arr decays to a pointer value only when used in an expression, and that decayed value is not a modifiable lvalue, so the compiler rejects arr++; the independently declared pointer p, by contrast, is a genuine modifiable lvalue, so p++ is accepted and simply advances p by one int width.

  3. Subscript-identity check: by the standard's own definition, arr[i] unfolds to *((arr) + (i)), i.e. *(arr + i), for every valid index i — a textual grammar definition mandated by the language, not a coincidence of a particular compiler.

Cross-check: Plug in a second, independent index to confirm the identity from rule 3: for i = 0, arr[0] and *(arr + 0) (which is *arr) both name the first element — the same equivalence holds at every index, matching the standard's unconditional grammar definition rather than depending on any particular i. Rules 1 and 2 similarly hold at every platform and index: an array's total size is never mandated to equal a pointer's size, and a decayed array name is never a modifiable lvalue, regardless of array length or platform.

Result: The statement that is TRUE about arrays and pointers in C is that array[i] is equivalent to *(array + i) — a mandated grammar definition in the C standard (C11 §6.5.2.1), independent of platform, compiler, or the specific index used.

title: What is the output of the following program #include <stdio.h>
subject: C Programming
text:
What is the output of the following program ?

#include <stdio.h>
int f (int *a, int n)
{
    if(n<=0) return 0;
    else if (*a%2 == 0) return *a + f(a+1, n-1);
    else return *a - f(a+1, n-1);
}
int main(void)
{
    int a[] = {12, 7, 13, 4, 11, 6};
    printf("%d", f(a,6));
    return 0;
}
solution:
Concept

This is non-tail recursion: each call has a pending add or subtract that runs AFTER the recursive call beneath it returns. The rule per element is: if the element is even, return element + (recursive result of the rest); if odd, return element - (recursive result of the rest); the base case (n<=0) returns 0. Because the recursive result is nested inside the next sign, the signs do NOT distribute independently over the elements - they compound as the stack unwinds.

Why naive parity-sum fails

It is tempting to just add every even element and subtract every odd element: (12+4+6) - (7+13+11) = 22 - 31 = -9. That is wrong, because the subtraction applies to the WHOLE remaining recursive result, not to a single element. The correct evaluation must unwind from the deepest call outward.

Trace (deepest call first)

  1. f(a+6, 0): base case, returns 0.

  2. f(a+5, 1): element 6 is even -> 6 + 0 = 6.

  3. f(a+4, 2): element 11 is odd -> 11 - 6 = 5.

  4. f(a+3, 3): element 4 is even -> 4 + 5 = 9.

  5. f(a+2, 4): element 13 is odd -> 13 - 9 = 4.

  6. f(a+1, 5): element 7 is odd -> 7 - 4 = 3.

  7. f(a, 6): element 12 is even -> 12 + 3 = 15.

Cross-check

Expand the nesting in one line: 12 + (7 - (13 - (4 + (11 - (6 + 0))))) = 12 + (7 - (13 - (4 + (11 - 6)))) = 12 + (7 - (13 - (4 + 5))) = 12 + (7 - (13 - 9)) = 12 + (7 - 4) = 12 + 3 = 15. The program prints 15.

optionFeedback.html: -9 is the parity-sum shortcut: adding all even elements and subtracting all odd elements, (12+4+6) - (7+13+11) = 22 - 31. That treats each sign as acting on a single element, but each odd element actually subtracts the entire nested result beneath it, so this shortcut does not match how the recursion unwinds.

5 is the value of one inner sub-call, namely 11 - 6 = 5 at the stage that begins from element 11. Reporting it as the final output means the recursion was unwound only partway and the remaining outer elements were never folded back in.
12 + (7 - (13 - (4 + (11 - 6)))) = 12 + 3. Even elements add the nested result and odd elements subtract it, evaluated from the base case outward, which is exactly what the code does.

19 comes from losing one of the nested sign flips while unwinding - for example treating an odd element as adding the result below it instead of subtracting it. Once any single +/- on a nested call is mistaken, the compounded total drifts away from what the code computes.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q69
subject: C Programming
text: In C, which statement about static inside a function is correct?

options.html: It is initialized every time function is called

solution:
In C, storage classes determine a variable's storage duration (lifetime), scope, and default initial value. The static keyword, when applied to a local variable inside a function, changes its storage duration from automatic (tied to entering and leaving the enclosing block) to static storage duration — a duration that spans the entire execution of the program, independent of how many times the enclosing function is called.

  1. The C standard guarantees only that a static-duration object's storage persists for the entire program execution, independent of how many times the enclosing function is called; in a typical implementation this guarantee is realized by giving the variable a fixed address in the program's static data/BSS area, separate from the transient per-call storage (commonly called the "stack") used for ordinary automatic variables — the segment names themselves are implementation detail, but the persistence they provide is standard-guaranteed.

  2. The standard also guarantees that its initializer — whose value for an object of static storage duration must be fixed at compile time (a constant expression, a string literal, or for aggregates a brace-enclosed list of such values) — takes effect exactly once, before the program begins running, rather than as a repeated action each time the enclosing block is entered; in practice this is usually realized by baking the initial value directly into the program's loaded image.

  3. Because of this, on every call after the first, the declaration line does not act as a re-initializing assignment: the variable keeps whatever value the previous call left it with — the standard-guaranteed behavior that makes static locals useful for building counters that persist across calls.

  4. Its value can still be modified inside the function like any ordinary variable — the static storage-class specifier does not by itself imply const; only an explicit const qualifier, which this declaration does not have, would prevent modification.

Trace a two-call sequence: on call 1, count goes from 0 to 1 — a change the standard guarantees will persist because of the object's static storage duration; on call 2, count starts already at 1 (not reinitialized to 0), confirming the lifetime spans the whole program rather than a single call. This also rules out treating it as an ordinary automatic-storage-duration object (whose duration the standard defines as ending when execution of the enclosing block ends, commonly realized via a call stack though the standard itself does not mandate that implementation) and rules out implicit immutability (nothing about static storage duration implies const).

optionFeedback.html: Storage duration is the standard's term for how long an object's storage is guaranteed to exist; understanding it well means distinguishing 'lifetime' (a runtime persistence property) from 'scope' (a compile-time, textual-visibility property) — two objects can share one of these while differing in the other.

An initializer is the part of a declaration written after '=' that supplies an object's starting value. C also permits designated initializers for aggregate types (arrays and structures), letting specific elements or members be set by name rather than by position.

Tools that report a 'stack trace' or a 'stack overflow' are referring to the call stack — the region that records the chain of currently active function calls; exhausting it through very deep recursion or oversized per-call data is a common runtime failure distinct from an ordinary out-of-memory error.

C recognizes two type qualifiers, const and volatile, that can be attached to a declared type; for pointer declarations the qualifier can independently apply to the pointer itself or to the type it points to, giving rise to combinations such as a constant pointer to non-constant data, or a pointer to constant data.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 16
subject: C Programming
text: Which of the following does not represent a valid storage class in C?
solution:
Concept

A storage-class specifier in C controls two things about an identifier: its storage duration (how long its storage exists) and its linkage (whether the same identifier refers to one shared entity across files). auto, register, static, and extern are the four specifiers conventionally taught together in introductory C (this 2009-era question predates the standard revision that later added a thread-storage specifier) as “the storage classes.” A type specifier — such as int, struct, or union — is a completely different category: it describes only the kind of data an identifier holds, never its duration or linkage.

Application

  1. Check automatic (the keyword auto): every plain local declaration already has this storage class by default, giving it block-scoped, automatic storage duration — one of the four storage classes.

  2. Check static: it gives a variable duration lasting the whole program run and, at file scope, restricts its linkage to that translation unit — also one of the four storage classes.

  3. Check extern: ordinarily it gives a declaration external linkage, letting it refer to a definition that exists elsewhere (unless it redeclares an identifier that already has internal linkage from an earlier declaration in the same file) — also one of the four storage classes.

  4. Check union: it controls neither duration nor linkage — it is a type specifier defining an aggregate type whose members overlap in memory. It is not a storage class at all.

So among the four options, only union fails to name a storage class — it belongs to the type-specifier category instead.

Cross-check

The C89/C99 grammar underlying this exam confirms this independently: the storage-class-specifier production groups auto | register | static | extern | typedef — but typedef only introduces a type alias and creates no storage at all, which is why introductory treatments still count just auto/register/static/extern as “the four storage classes.” union, by contrast, has always sat under the separate type-specifier production (alongside void, char, int, struct-or-union-specifier, enum-specifier, …), never under storage-class-specifier — confirming again that it is the one option that does not represent a valid storage class.

optionFeedback.html: auto gives a variable automatic storage duration: its storage exists only for the lifetime of the enclosing block, and the standard does not mandate any particular mechanism — a stack frame, a machine register, or anything else — for holding it during that time.

static gives a variable static storage duration, so a single copy persists for the entire program run — zero-initialized by default and retaining its value across function calls — and, when applied to a file-scope identifier, additionally restricts that identifier to internal linkage within its own translation unit.

union defines a type whose members all occupy the same region of storage, so writing through one member can change what another member reads back; the type’s overall size is at least as large as its largest member, though alignment requirements may add padding beyond that.

extern ordinarily gives a declaration external linkage, referring to a definition placed elsewhere without allocating storage of its own — except when redeclaring an already-internal-linkage identifier (which keeps that prior linkage) or supplying its own initializer (which makes that declaration a definition in its own right).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q150
subject: C Programming
text: Which of the following is used for dynamic memory allocation in C?
solution:
Concept

In the C programming language, memory needed at runtime (rather than fixed at compile time) is managed through standard library functions declared in the header stdlib.h — malloc(), calloc(), and realloc() for allocation, and free() for deallocation. C has no dedicated operators for this; only C++ adds the new and delete operators, which additionally invoke a constructor or destructor as part of allocation/deallocation.

Application

  1. Declare a pointer variable of the required type, for example int *ptr;

  2. Call malloc with the number of bytes needed, for example ptr = malloc(5 * sizeof(int));

  3. malloc reserves a block of uninitialised memory of that size on the heap and returns a void pointer to it (or a null pointer if the request cannot be satisfied), which is assigned or cast to the pointer type.

  4. The allocated block is used through ptr, and later released with free(ptr); when it is no longer needed.

Cross-check

  • new and delete are operators defined only by the C++ language specification; a standard C compiler does not recognise them as memory-management constructs.

  • create is not defined anywhere in the C (or C++) standard library as a memory-management construct.

  • Among the four given options, only malloc is a valid C construct for dynamic memory allocation, matching ISO C’s specification of malloc in stdlib.h.

optionFeedback.html: new is an operator that C++ provides for combining memory allocation for an object on the free store with an automatic call to that object's constructor within the same expression.
delete is an operator that C++ provides for combining release of memory previously obtained via new with an automatic call to the object's destructor.

create is used across various libraries and frameworks as a factory-method or constructor-helper identifier, with its exact behavior defined independently by whichever library or framework provides it.

malloc is a function that the C standard library provides (declared in stdlib.h) for reserving a block of uninitialised memory of a specified byte size on the heap, returning a pointer to it, to be released later with the paired free function.

Dynamic memory allocation lets a program request storage while it is running, when the required size or lifetime is not known at compile time.

In C, allocation functions are declared in the standard header <stdlib.h>, and allocated storage is accessed through a pointer.

Application

Consider reserving space for five integers at runtime.

  1. Compute the required size as 5 * sizeof(int).

  2. Call int *p = malloc(5 * sizeof *p);. The function requests one contiguous block of that many bytes and returns its starting address as a void * pointer, which C converts to int * on assignment.

  3. Check p != NULL before using the block, because allocation can fail.

  4. After use, call free(p); so the dynamically allocated block is released.

  • alloc() is not an ISO C standard-library allocation function.

  • create() is not an ISO C standard-library memory function; system APIs may use that name for other resources.

  • new is a C++ allocation operator rather than a C function named new().

  • malloc() is declared by ISO C for requesting a block of storage of a specified byte size.

Therefore, the required function is malloc().

title: Consider the following code snippet: #include <stdio.h> int main() FILE
subject: C Programming
text:
Consider the following C code snippet:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {

   FILE *file = fopen("example.txt", "r");

   if (file == NULL) {
       printf("Error opening file. ");
       return 1;
   }

   int ch;

   while ((ch = fgetc(file)) != EOF) {
       putchar(ch);
   }

   if (feof(file)) {
       printf(" End of file reached. ");
   }

   fclose(file);

   return 0;
}

What is the purpose of the feof(file) function call in this program?

options.html: To read the next character from the file stream
To determine whether the end-of-file indicator for the file stream has been set
To close the file after all characters are read
To move the file pointer to the beginning of the file
To open the file in read mode

solution:
Concept

In C's standard I/O library, each open stream keeps two status flags: an end-of-file (EOF) indicator and an error indicator. A read function does NOT set the EOF indicator merely by returning the EOF value; the indicator is set only after an attempt to read past the last byte actually fails. feof is a pure test: it returns non-zero if the EOF indicator for that stream is currently set, and zero otherwise. It inspects a flag; it neither reads data nor moves the file position.

Applying it to this program

  1. The loop while ((ch = fgetc(file)) != EOF) keeps reading one character at a time and printing it. fgetc returns the character as an int, or the macro EOF when no more characters can be read.

  2. The loop exits when fgetc returns EOF. That return value alone is ambiguous: it can mean a genuine end-of-file OR a read error.

  3. To disambiguate, the program calls feof(file). If it returns non-zero, the EOF indicator is set, so the stream really reached its end, and the program prints the end-of-file message.

Cross-check / contrast

  • Reading the next character is the job of fgetc / getc, which return the byte and advance the position; a status-test function returns no data.

  • Closing the stream is done by fclose, which flushes and releases the stream.

  • Repositioning to the start is done by rewind or fseek(file, 0, SEEK_SET); a status test never moves the position.

  • Opening in read mode is done by fopen("...", "r"), which happens before any reading.

Therefore feof(file) exists to report whether the end-of-file indicator for the stream has been set — a status query used here to confirm the loop ended because the file was fully read.

optionFeedback.html: Reading and returning the next byte while advancing the file position is the job of fgetc or getc — the functions that actually consume characters inside the loop. Treating this call as a way to fetch the next character confuses a separate operation that produces data and moves the position with one that does neither.

The end-of-file indicator is a per-stream status flag that becomes set only after a read attempt runs out of data, and feof returns non-zero exactly when that flag is set for the given stream. Because fgetc returning EOF could mean either a true end-of-file or a read error, this check is what distinguishes the two after the loop — making 'reporting whether the end-of-file indicator has been set' the precise role of the call.

Closing the file — flushing its buffers and releasing the stream — is performed by fclose, which the program calls separately on the line after this check. Reading this call as the closing step mistakes it for the cleanup that fclose carries out; the stream remains open here.

Moving the file pointer back to the start is done with rewind or fseek(file, 0, SEEK_SET) — functions whose purpose is to change the current file position. This call issues no such repositioning, so reading it as a seek-to-start confuses it with those positioning functions.

Opening the file in read mode is the job of fopen("example.txt", "r"), which runs once at the top of the program before the loop. This call is reached only after the file is already open, so treating it as the open step mistakes it for the earlier fopen call.
